notes: How this game's places are lit.
The settings screen says what you want everywhere. This file says what a
particular place wants, and where it gives an answer, that answer is the
one in force there. Which file is in force is chosen on the settings
screen, under Game config; choose None, or take this file out of the
folder, and every map falls back to the settings alone.
As it ships this file changes nothing. It states no value and names no
map, so the picture is exactly the settings screen's own. Everything
below is here to be read and filled in.
JSON has no comments, so anything written under a key called "notes" is
the documentation: at any level, as one line or as a list of them, and
never read as data. It is a reserved name that no part of this file will
ever use for anything else.
A file that is not JSON at all costs the whole file -- one missing brace
moves every following line into a different place, so nothing is loaded
and whatever was in force stays in force. Anything else costs only
itself: an unknown key, a value out of range or a colour that is not six
hexadecimal digits is reported, that key is ignored, and the rest of the
file is read.
Angles are in degrees. Distances are in world units.
What every map gets, including the maps nobody lists below.
"settings" holds settings-screen keys, spelled exactly as the settings
file spells them and read by exactly the same rules -- so every bound
and every complaint comes from the settings screen itself, and the two
can never disagree. A key belongs here when it says how a PLACE is lit
rather than what a SCREEN wants: the shading and the whole light rig
may be written here, and the brightness and contrast of the picture may
not. For example:
"settings": {
"shading_mode": "modern",
"room_light_reach": 0.85,
"player_light_intensity": 0.4,
"player_light_flicker": true,
"ambient_color": "#576180"
"lights" says what particular THINGS give off, under "graphics", keyed
by the graphic the map draws them with -- for where one value for a
whole map is not enough, such as a brazier that should read brighter
than a table candle. Nothing has to be listed for a map's torches to
work: the game already marks them, custom maps included.
"lights": {
"graphics": {
"colour": "#ffb46e" },
Each field stands on its own, so a map may raise a strength without
restating a colour. "off" is the whole entry rather than a field: a
thing the map marks unshaded that is plainly not a light -- a glowing
decal, a bright pickup -- is refused outright.
Under the same "lights", "surfaces" says what a painted SURFACE gives
off -- lava, a glowing rune, a lit sigil on a wall -- keyed by the
texture number the map's own geometry carries for a face. It belongs
here as readily as under a map: a texture is the same texture wherever
it is painted, so a game whose lava glows usually wants it to glow
everywhere.
"lights": {
"surfaces": {
"0x0a31": { "colour": "#ff5a20", "strength": 1.2,
"reach": 640 }
The colour is REQUIRED here, and that is the one way a surface differs
from a thing. A thing is drawn as a cut-out sprite, so the flame can be
told from the bracket it hangs on and the light's colour read off it; a
wall texture is cut out of nothing, so the same reading over lava
returns the colour of the rock around it. Rather than quietly give
every glowing surface in the game one fixed colour, a grant with no
colour lights nothing and says so. Write it once here and a map may
raise the strength without restating it.
A grant lights the room; it does not repaint the surface. Whether a
face is drawn fullbright stays what the map itself says. One light is
placed per room per texture, in the middle of that room's granted faces
and just clear of them, so a lake of lava is one light over the lake
rather than three hundred fighting for the few slots the picture
carries.
Running the game with HWR_OBJ_DUMP set to a file name writes out every
object a map holds: its own number in the first column, then the
graphic it is drawn with and the id tag its creator gave it. That is
where these numbers come from, and they are the same numbers the ROTH
Editor shows for the same object. See "maps" below: one particular
object is described under the map it stands in, never here.
One entry per place, keyed by the name of the map's OWN file, without
the folder and without the extension: STUDY1, CRYPT1, TOWER1. The name
is matched whatever its case and with or without an extension, so
"study1" and "STUDY1.RAW" name one map. Maps that share a texture
archive are still different maps here. A map nobody lists gets
"everywhere" alone, silently, so a map pack is covered whether or not
anyone has described it.
A map's entry has the SAME shape as "everywhere" above, and that is the
whole of the composition rule: a map's answer is laid over the game's
answer, field by field.
"STUDY1": {
"notes": "Lamplit and enclosed; its own candles carry it.",
"settings": { "room_light_reach": 0.72 },
"lights": { "graphics": { "0x0412": { "strength": 2.0 } } }
A row a map answers for is marked on the settings screen with what the
map says, because moving that setting will not change the picture where
you are standing.
Under "lights" a map may also describe ONE PARTICULAR OBJECT of it
rather than a kind of them -- the hearth in one room, not every brazier
in the game. Each entry names its object THE WAY THE ROTH EDITOR NAMES
IT, so the numbers you write are the numbers you are reading off your
screen while you write them. Two ways, and an entry uses exactly one:
"index": N   the object's own number, which the editor shows as
"Object: N" when you select it. It names one thing.
"id": N      the tag the editor shows as "ID:", which the map's
creator typed to gather objects into a group for the
command system. It is MEANT to be shared, so this
applies to every object carrying that tag -- which is
how a corridor of torches is tuned in one line. An id
of 0 is refused: it is the untagged default that most
objects carry.
"STUDY1": {
"lights": {
"objects": [
{ "notes": "the hearth",
"index": 12,
"strength": 2.6, "reach": 700,
"colour": "#ff9040" },
{ "notes": "every torch the author tagged alike",
{ "notes": "a bright decal, not a light",
"index": 40, "off": true }
What one entry says wins over whatever "graphics" said about its kind,
and an "index" entry wins over an "id" entry -- the most specific
statement anybody made is the one in force -- and all three compose
field by field, so one hearth may be made stronger than the group it is
tagged with without restating the colour its kind already has. "off"
is the whole entry here too: turning one object off leaves every other
object of its kind and its group alight, and naming one object in a map
whose whole kind is "off" makes that one a light again.
NUMBERS MOVE WHEN A MAP IS EDITED. An object's number is its position
in the map's own list, so deleting an object in the editor shifts the
number of every object after it. For a finished map "index" is exact
and stable; for a map still being built the ID TAG is the stable
handle, because it travels with the object it was typed on.
A "graphic" may be written beside either. It is a CHECK rather than
part of the address: beside an "index", where the object with that
number is drawn with something else the entry is still applied and the
game says so; beside an "id", where NO object carrying that tag is
drawn with it. That is how a file written for one version of a map
tells you it has gone stale. An entry naming a number nothing answers
to says so too, once, naming the map -- so a mistyped number is
visible rather than quietly doing nothing.
And under the same "lights", "placed" hangs a light that belongs to
NO object at all, at three numbers you choose because there is nothing
standing there to tune:
"STUDY1": {
"lights": {
"placed": [
{ "notes": "a lamp over the stairwell",
"colour": "#ffb46e",
"strength": 1.2, "reach": 420 }
"at" and "colour" are both required. Take the three numbers from
HWR_OBJ_DUMP rather than from the ROTH Editor's position boxes: the
editor displays X with the opposite sign to the one the map file
carries, so an X copied off its screen puts the light on the wrong
side of the world. Y and Z agree.
The colour is required for the same reason a surface's is: there is
nothing to read one off. A torch
is a cut-out sprite the game can take a colour from; a light hanging in
the air has no sprite, no object and no map mark, so an entry without a
colour lights nothing and says so. "strength" and "reach" fall to the
settings screen where they are left out. There is no "off": an entry
here exists only because you wrote it, so delete the line.
Each one is placed in whichever of the map's rooms contains the point,
which is the same question the editor asks when you drop an object into
a room, and is then held by the same containments as every other light.
One hung outside every room lights nothing and says so.
Both lists belong to ONE map and are written under it, never under
"everywhere": an object's number is a number in one map's own list,
and the same three numbers in another map are a different corner of a
different building.
